question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Bombay — Acquisition & Location]
options: Bombay is located on the western coast of India, on a group of islands on the Arabian Sea
Bombay was received by England as part of the dowry when King Charles II married Catherine of Braganza in 1661
The English East India Company received Bombay from the English Crown in 1668 for an annual rent of £10
Bombay is situated at the mouth of the Godavari River, providing access to the Deccan
wrong_fact: Bombay is NOT situated at the mouth of the Godavari River. The Godavari empties into the Bay of Bengal near Rajamahendravaram (Rajahmundry) in Andhra Pradesh — on the eastern coast. Bombay is on the western coast of India, on a natural deep-water harbour on Mahim Bay/Thane Creek, not at any major river delta.
explanation: Bombay (Mumbai) consists of a peninsula/island group on the Arabian Sea coast of Maharashtra. The Portuguese ceded it to Charles II of England as Catherine of Braganza's dowry in 1661; the Crown then leased it to the EIC in 1668 for £10 per annum. Its strategic value lay in its excellent deep-water natural harbour, not in river access. The Godavari is a major east-coast river.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Bombay — Presidency & Administrative Importance]
options: The English East India Company shifted its western India headquarters from Surat to Bombay in 1687
Bombay became the seat of the Bombay Presidency, which at its largest extent included parts of present-day Maharashtra, Gujarat, and Sind
Gerald Aungier, Governor of Bombay (1669–1677), developed Bombay into a flourishing trading settlement
Bombay Presidency was established earlier than the Madras Presidency, making it the oldest English presidency in India
wrong_fact: Bombay Presidency was NOT the oldest English presidency. The Madras Presidency (Fort St. George) was established in 1639–1640, earlier than Bombay's formal presidency status. The Bengal Presidency (Fort William) was formalised in 1700. Bombay became the western headquarters only in 1687. Madras is recognised as the oldest of the three presidencies.
explanation: Gerald Aungier's governorship (1669–77) transformed Bombay by developing its port, judiciary, and civic institutions. The EIC moved its western HQ from Surat to Bombay in 1687. The Bombay Presidency eventually covered Maharashtra, Gujarat, Sind, and parts of Karnataka. However, the Madras Presidency (Fort St. George, 1640) pre-dates Bombay's elevation as a presidency capital.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Bombay — Islands, Harbour & Maratha Wars]
options: Bombay was originally composed of seven islands — Bombay, Colaba, Old Woman's Island, Mahim, Mazagaon, Parel, and Worli — that were later connected by land reclamation
Bombay's Thane Creek and Mahim Bay provided a sheltered anchorage superior to the open roadstead of Surat
The First Anglo-Maratha War (1775–82) ended with the Treaty of Salbai, under which Bombay ceded Salsette Island to the Marathas
Salsette Island, adjacent to Bombay, was seized by the English from the Portuguese in 1774 before the First Anglo-Maratha War
wrong_fact: The Treaty of Salbai (1782) did NOT result in the English ceding Salsette to the Marathas. By the Treaty of Salbai, the status quo was largely restored, but the English retained Salsette Island — which they had seized from the Portuguese in 1774. The Marathas did NOT regain Salsette. The treaty mainly confirmed English possession of Salsette.
explanation: Bombay's seven islands were gradually unified by causeways and reclamation (completed largely by the 19th century). Thane Creek provided a sheltered anchorage unavailable at Surat. The English captured Salsette (north of Bombay) from the Portuguese in 1774, triggering Maratha hostility. The First Anglo-Maratha War (1775–82) ended with the Treaty of Salbai, which restored pre-war territories but confirmed British retention of Salsette — the opposite of what Option C claims.
